lessons.title: Pressure and pressure differences in fluids
lessons.summary: Calculate pressure using p = F/A, explain how pressure in a liquid changes with depth and density using p = hρg, understand why objects float or sink because of upthrust, and describe how atmospheric pressure changes with height.
objectives: I can calculate pressure at a surface using p = F / A.
I can explain that a fluid exerts pressure at right angles to any surface and that pressure in a liquid increases with depth and density.
I can calculate the pressure due to a column of liquid using p = h ρ g (Higher).
I can explain upthrust in terms of a pressure difference and use it to explain floating and sinking (Higher).
I can describe the atmosphere and explain why atmospheric pressure decreases with height.

activities.title: Pressure at a surface
activities.content:
## What is pressure?

A **fluid** is anything that can flow: a **liquid** or a **gas**. Fluids push on every surface they touch because their particles are constantly colliding with it. The force from a fluid always acts **at right angles (normal)** to the surface.

**Pressure** is the force acting per unit area:

$$p = \frac{F}{A}$$

- $p$ = pressure in **pascals (Pa)**
- $F$ = force acting normal to the surface, in **newtons (N)**
- $A$ = area the force acts on, in **square metres (m²)**

One pascal is one newton per square metre: **1 Pa = 1 N/m²**. Because a pascal is tiny, pressures are often quoted in kPa (1000 Pa).

### Same force, different pressure
A drawing pin pushed with 10 N spreads that force over the flat head (large area, low pressure on your thumb) but concentrates it on the sharp point (tiny area, enormous pressure) so it pierces the board. Snow shoes work the other way: they spread your weight over a large area so the pressure is too small to sink into the snow.

### Units check
Areas in cm² must be converted to m²: divide by 10 000. For example 25 cm² = 0.0025 m².

activities.title: Worked example: pressure from a box
activities.content:
**A box of weight 480 N rests on the floor. Its base measures 0.8 m by 0.6 m. Calculate the pressure on the floor.**

Area $= 0.8 \times 0.6 = 0.48$ m²

$p = \dfrac{F}{A} = \dfrac{480}{0.48} = 1000$ Pa

**The box is tipped onto its side, where the face measures 0.6 m by 0.5 m. What is the new pressure?**

Area $= 0.6 \times 0.5 = 0.30$ m²

$p = \dfrac{480}{0.30} = 1600$ Pa

The weight has not changed, but a smaller area means a larger pressure.

**Rearranging.** A hydraulic press produces a pressure of 2 × 10⁶ Pa on a piston of area 0.05 m². The force is:

$F = pA = 2 \times 10^6 \times 0.05 = 100\,000$ N

question.text: An elephant's foot has an area of 0.10 m². The elephant has a weight of 40 000 N spread equally over its four feet. Calculate the pressure under one foot.
question.hint: First find the force on one foot (a quarter of the weight), then use p = F ÷ A.

activities.title: Pressure in a liquid
activities.content:
## Pressure increases with depth

Dive to the bottom of a swimming pool and your ears hurt. The deeper you go, the more water there is above you pressing down, so the **pressure increases with depth**.

Pressure in a liquid also depends on the **density** of the liquid. A denser liquid has more mass in each cubic metre, so a column of it has more weight and exerts more pressure. Sea water (about 1030 kg/m³) creates slightly more pressure at a given depth than fresh water (1000 kg/m³).

### The pressure equation (Higher tier)
$$p = h \rho g$$

- $p$ = pressure due to the column of liquid, in **Pa**
- $h$ = **height** (depth) of the column, in **m**
- $\rho$ (rho) = **density** of the liquid, in **kg/m³**
- $g$ = gravitational field strength, **9.8 N/kg**

This gives the *extra* pressure from the liquid. The **total** pressure at that depth is the liquid pressure **plus atmospheric pressure** on the surface (about 100 kPa).

### Why the equation works
Imagine a column of liquid of height $h$ and cross-sectional area $A$ above a point. Its volume is $Ah$, its mass is $\rho A h$ and its weight is $\rho A h g$. Pressure = weight ÷ area = $\rho A h g / A = h \rho g$. The area cancels, which is why the pressure at a given depth is the same in a narrow pipe as in a wide lake.

Pressure in a liquid acts **in all directions**, not just downwards. That is why water squirts sideways out of a hole in a bucket, and why the lowest hole squirts furthest.

activities.title: Worked example: pressure at depth
activities.content:
**A diver is 12 m below the surface of a lake. The density of the water is 1000 kg/m³. Calculate the pressure due to the water on the diver. (g = 9.8 N/kg)**

$p = h \rho g = 12 \times 1000 \times 9.8 = 117\,600$ Pa ≈ 118 kPa

**What is the total pressure on the diver if atmospheric pressure is 101 kPa?**

Total $= 117.6 + 101 = 218.6$ kPa, roughly **twice** atmospheric pressure.

**The diver moves to the sea (density 1030 kg/m³) at the same depth.**

$p = 12 \times 1030 \times 9.8 = 121\,128$ Pa ≈ 121 kPa

A denser liquid gives a higher pressure at the same depth.

**Rearranging for depth.** A pressure gauge in fresh water reads 49 000 Pa above atmospheric. How deep is it?

$h = \dfrac{p}{\rho g} = \dfrac{49\,000}{1000 \times 9.8} = 5.0$ m

question.text: A fish tank is filled with water of density 1000 kg/m³ to a depth of 0.45 m. Calculate the pressure due to the water at the bottom of the tank. Use g = 9.8 N/kg.
question.hint: p = h ρ g. Multiply depth × density × g.

question.text: Which TWO of the following would increase the pressure at the bottom of a container of liquid?
question.hint: Look at the variables in p = h ρ g.
question.explanation: Pressure depends on depth (h) and density (ρ). Making the container wider does not change the pressure at a given depth because the area cancels, and using a smaller container of the same depth changes nothing either.

options.text: Filling the container to a greater depth
Replacing the liquid with a denser one
Using a wider container filled to the same depth
options.feedback: Width does not matter: pressure depends on depth and density only.

options.text: Painting the container a darker colour

activities.title: Upthrust and floating (Higher)
activities.content:
## Why do things float?

When an object is submerged in a fluid, the pressure on its **bottom surface is greater** than on its **top surface** because the bottom is deeper. The larger upward force on the bottom minus the smaller downward force on the top leaves a net **upward force** on the object. This force is called **upthrust**.

**Upthrust is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the object.** A brick that pushes aside 2 N of water experiences 2 N of upthrust. This is why a very heavy ship can float: its hull is shaped to displace a huge volume of water.

### Floating or sinking
Compare the object's **weight** with the **maximum upthrust** it can get when fully submerged:

| Comparison | What happens |
|---|---|
| Weight < upthrust when fully submerged | object rises and **floats**, sitting partly out of the water until upthrust = weight |
| Weight = upthrust | object stays put at any depth (neutral buoyancy, like a submarine trimmed perfectly) |
| Weight > upthrust | object **sinks** |

A quicker test uses **density**: an object **less dense** than the fluid floats; one **more dense** sinks. A solid steel ball (density about 8000 kg/m³) sinks in water, but the same steel shaped into a hollow hull has an average density lower than water and floats.

### Partially submerged objects
A floating object displaces just enough fluid so that the upthrust exactly balances its weight. Load a boat with cargo and it sits lower in the water to displace more, increasing the upthrust.

question.text: A solid block has a weight of 8 N. When fully submerged in water it displaces water with a weight of 5 N. What happens to the block?
question.hint: Compare the weight of the block with the upthrust (the weight of water displaced).
question.explanation: Upthrust = weight of water displaced = 5 N. This is less than the block's weight of 8 N, so there is a resultant downward force and the block sinks.

options.text: It sinks because the upthrust (5 N) is less than its weight (8 N)
It floats because it displaces water
options.feedback: Displacing water is not enough; the upthrust must be at least equal to the weight.

options.text: It stays at any depth because the forces are balanced
It rises because the upthrust is 8 N

activities.title: Atmospheric pressure
activities.content:
## The atmosphere

The **atmosphere** is a thin layer of air, a few hundred kilometres thick, surrounding the Earth. The air is a fluid, so it exerts pressure on everything in it. At sea level **atmospheric pressure is about 100 kPa** (100 000 N on every square metre!). We do not notice because the pressure inside our bodies pushes back equally.

### Where the pressure comes from
Air is made of **particles** in constant random motion. When they **collide with a surface** they exert a force on it. Atmospheric pressure is the total effect of billions of these collisions every second.

### Why atmospheric pressure decreases with height
As you go **higher**:
- there is **less air above** you, so the weight of the column of air pressing down is smaller,
- the air becomes **less dense** (the atmosphere gets thinner), so there are **fewer particles** per cubic metre and **fewer collisions** with a surface each second.

Both effects make the pressure fall. At the summit of Everest (about 8.8 km) the pressure is only about a third of the sea-level value, which is why climbers struggle to get enough oxygen.

Unlike water, the density of air is **not constant** with height, so the simple $p = h\rho g$ formula does not work for the whole atmosphere.

### Evidence for air pressure
Sucking the air out of a can makes it crumple: the outside air pressure is no longer balanced by the pressure inside.

question.text: Explain why atmospheric pressure is lower at the top of a mountain than at sea level.
question.hint: Think about how much air is above you and how tightly packed the particles are.
question.explanation: Higher up there is less air above, so the weight of air pressing down is smaller. The air is also less dense, so fewer particles collide with a surface each second.

markScheme.criterion: Less air above / smaller weight of air column pressing down
Air is less dense / fewer particles so fewer collisions per second

question.text: True or false: the pressure in a liquid at a given depth acts only downwards.
question.hint: Think about water spraying sideways from a hole in the side of a bucket.
question.explanation: False. Pressure in a fluid acts in all directions. It pushes at right angles to any surface, including upwards on the bottom of a submerged object (which gives upthrust).

options.text: True
False

question.text:
A submarine is at a depth of 200 m in sea water of density 1030 kg/m³. Use g = 9.8 N/kg.

(a) Calculate the pressure due to the sea water at this depth. (2 marks)

(b) A hatch on the submarine has an area of 0.60 m². Calculate the force from the water on the hatch. (2 marks)

(c) Explain, in terms of pressure, why the submarine experiences upthrust. (1 mark)
question.hint: For (b), rearrange p = F/A to F = p × A.
question.explanation: (a) p = h ρ g = 200 × 1030 × 9.8 = 2 018 800 Pa ≈ 2.0 × 10⁶ Pa. (b) F = p A = 2 018 800 × 0.60 = 1 211 280 N ≈ 1.2 × 10⁶ N. (c) The bottom of the submarine is deeper than the top, so the pressure on the bottom is greater; this pressure difference gives a net upward force.

markScheme.criterion: Substitution 200 × 1030 × 9.8
Pressure ≈ 2.0 × 10⁶ Pa (2 018 800 Pa)
Uses F = p × A
Force ≈ 1.2 × 10⁶ N
Pressure is greater on the bottom than on the top (deeper), giving a net upward force

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Pressure = force ÷ area**, $p = F/A$, in **pascals** (1 Pa = 1 N/m²). Fluids push at right angles to surfaces.
- Pressure in a liquid **increases with depth and density** and acts in **all directions**.
- (Higher) $p = h\rho g$ gives the pressure due to a column of liquid; add atmospheric pressure for the total.
- (Higher) **Upthrust** is the net upward force from the pressure difference between the bottom and top of a submerged object; it equals the **weight of fluid displaced**. Objects float if they are less dense than the fluid.
- **Atmospheric pressure** (about 100 kPa at sea level) comes from air particle collisions and **decreases with height** because there is less air above and it is less dense.

practiceQuestions.text: Which unit is the same as one pascal?
practiceQuestions.explanation: 1 Pa = 1 N/m², one newton per square metre.

options.text: 1 N/m²
1 N m
1 N/kg
1 J/m²

practiceQuestions.text: A woman of weight 600 N stands on both feet. The total area of her shoes in contact with the ground is 0.030 m². Calculate the pressure on the ground.
A gas exerts a pressure of 150 000 Pa on a piston of area 0.0040 m². Calculate the force on the piston.
Calculate the pressure due to the liquid at a depth of 2.5 m in a tank of oil with density 850 kg/m³. Use g = 9.8 N/kg.
The pressure due to the water at the bottom of a reservoir is 294 000 Pa. The density of water is 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.8 N/kg. Calculate the depth of the water.
practiceQuestions.hint: Rearrange p = h ρ g to give h = p ÷ (ρ g).

metadata.blanksText: Upthrust on a submerged object is equal to the ___ of the fluid displaced. An object will float if its density is ___ than the density of the fluid.

practiceQuestions.hint: Think of Archimedes: what does the displaced fluid have that balances the object?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced. Objects less dense than the fluid float.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: atmospheric pressure is caused by air particles colliding with surfaces.
practiceQuestions.hint: What is air made of and what are its particles doing?
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Air particles move randomly and collide with surfaces, and the force from these collisions spread over the area is the pressure.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: Put these steps in order to explain why a submerged object experiences upthrust.
practiceQuestions.hint: Start with what pressure does as you go deeper.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Pressure increases with depth, so the bottom of the object is at a higher pressure than the top, giving a larger upward force than downward force, so there is a net upward force: upthrust.
order: Pressure in a liquid increases with depth
The bottom surface of the object is deeper than the top surface
The upward force on the bottom is larger than the downward force on the top
The difference between these forces is a net upward force called upthrust

practiceQuestions.text: A camel has very wide feet. Explain why this helps it walk on soft sand.
practiceQuestions.hint: Use the equation p = F ÷ A.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Wide feet spread the camel's weight over a larger area, so the pressure on the sand is smaller and the feet do not sink in as far.

markScheme.criterion: Larger area of contact with the sand
So pressure is lower and the feet sink less

practiceQuestions.text:
A cargo ship floats in a harbour. Cargo is loaded and the ship sits lower in the water.

(a) Explain why the ship floats even though it is made of steel, which is much denser than water. (2 marks)

(b) Explain why loading cargo makes the ship sit lower in the water. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the average density of the whole ship including the air inside, and about what upthrust must equal for a floating object.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) The hull is hollow and contains air, so the ship's average density is less than that of water; it displaces enough water for the upthrust to equal its weight. (b) The cargo increases the weight, so the ship needs more upthrust; it sinks lower to displace a greater weight of water until upthrust again equals the weight.

markScheme.criterion: The hull is hollow / contains air so the average density is less than water
It displaces enough water for the upthrust to equal its weight
Cargo increases the ship's weight, so more upthrust is needed
It sits lower to displace more water / a greater weight of water

practiceQuestions.text: A table has a weight of 240 N shared equally between its four legs. The base of each leg has an area of 0.0020 m². Calculate the pressure exerted on the floor by one leg.
practiceQuestions.hint: Find the force on one leg first (a quarter of the weight), then use p = F ÷ A.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Force on one leg = 240 ÷ 4 = 60 N. p = F ÷ A = 60 ÷ 0.0020 = 30 000 Pa (30 kPa).

practiceQuestions.text: A vat in a sweet factory is filled with syrup of density 1400 kg/m³ to a depth of 0.60 m. Calculate the pressure due to the syrup at the bottom of the vat. Use g = 9.8 N/kg.
practiceQuestions.hint: p = h ρ g. Multiply depth × density × gravitational field strength.

practiceQuestions.text: A diver swims down from the surface of the sea. Which TWO statements about the pressure due to the water are correct?
practiceQuestions.hint: Remember p = h ρ g: only depth and density appear in the equation.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Pressure increases with depth because there is more water above pushing down. Sea water is denser than fresh water, so at the same depth the pressure is greater in the sea. The width of the body of water makes no difference, and at 10 m the pressure is clearly higher than at the surface.

options.text: The pressure increases as the diver goes deeper
At a given depth the pressure is greater in sea water than in fresh water because sea water is denser
The pressure at a given depth depends on how wide the sea is
options.feedback: Width does not appear in p = h ρ g.

options.text: The pressure at a depth of 10 m is the same as at the surface

practiceQuestions.text: A toy boat has a weight of 3 N. When placed in a pond it settles at a level where it has displaced water weighing 3 N. What happens to the boat?
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare the upthrust (the weight of water displaced) with the weight of the boat.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Upthrust = weight of water displaced = 3 N, which equals the boat's weight. The forces are balanced, so the boat floats at that level.

options.text: It floats, because the upthrust (3 N) equals its weight (3 N)
It sinks, because it has displaced less water than its own volume
options.feedback: What matters is whether the upthrust can match the weight, and here it does.

options.text: It floats because plastic is always lighter than water
options.feedback: Floating depends on the upthrust equalling the weight, not on the material alone.

options.text: It rises completely out of the water because the upthrust pushes it up
options.feedback: If it rose it would displace less water, so the upthrust would fall below its weight.

practiceQuestions.text: A sealed packet of crisps is taken to the top of a high mountain. The packet swells up. Explain why.
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare the pressure of the air trapped inside the packet with the atmospheric pressure outside at the summit.
practiceQuestions.explanation: At the top of the mountain there is less air above, and the air is less dense, so atmospheric pressure is lower than at the bottom. The gas sealed inside the packet still pushes outwards at its original pressure, which is now greater than the pressure of the air pushing inwards, so the packet expands.

markScheme.criterion: Atmospheric pressure is lower at the summit because there is less air above / air is less dense
The gas inside pushes outwards with a greater pressure than the air outside pushes in, so the packet expands

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: a sealed, empty drinks can lowered deep into a lake is squeezed from every side, not just from above.
practiceQuestions.hint: In which directions does the pressure in a liquid act on a surface?
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Pressure in a fluid acts in all directions, at right angles to every surface it touches. The can is pushed inwards on its sides and bottom as well as its top.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text:
A dam holds back a reservoir of fresh water of density 1000 kg/m³. An inspection hatch in the dam wall is 25 m below the water surface and has an area of 0.50 m². Use g = 9.8 N/kg.

(a) Calculate the pressure due to the water at the hatch. (2 marks)

(b) Calculate the force from the water on the hatch. (2 marks)

(c) Explain, in terms of pressure, why the dam wall is built much thicker at the bottom than at the top. (1 mark)
practiceQuestions.hint: For (b), rearrange p = F/A to give F = p × A.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) p = h ρ g = 25 × 1000 × 9.8 = 245 000 Pa. (b) F = p A = 245 000 × 0.50 = 122 500 N ≈ 1.2 × 10⁵ N. (c) Pressure increases with depth, so the water pushes on the bottom of the wall with a much greater pressure (and force) than on the top; the wall must be thicker there to withstand it.

markScheme.criterion: Substitution 25 × 1000 × 9.8
Pressure = 245 000 Pa
Uses F = p × A
Pressure is greater at the bottom because it is deeper, so the force on the lower wall is larger
